summary:
Faroe Islands stands under Denmark's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here. The territory is self-governing within the Realm of Denmark; equality and family law are made locally, beneath a Danish human-rights framework.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Faroe Islands since 1933, when it was decriminalised across the Kingdom of Denmark. The age of consent was then set at 18 for male same-sex relations, and the territory did not follow Denmark's 1977 move to a gender-neutral age of 15 until 1988.

The only criminal penalty touching LGBT people in the sourced material sits in the anti-discrimination law: anyone who publicly makes a statement that threatens, insults or degrades a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation is liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. That provision took effect on 1 January 2007, making the Faroe Islands the last Northern European country to prohibit discrimination and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation.

Same-sex marriage was adopted locally in 2017, late for the Nordics and after friction between church and state.

Physical violence against LGBT people is on the record. In 2006 the openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls. Police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later admitted to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, and died by suicide in 2012. In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in Tórshavn; the group was attacked nowhere else on its tour.

Religiously and politically motivated opposition sits openly in Faroese politics. On 7 September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic prime minister Johanna Sigurdardóttir and her partner, citing his religion. In July 2015 he demanded that Pride be banned from its position two days before the national holiday; singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him, and his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality.

No trans-specific incident, charge or legal restriction appears in the sourced material. The recorded hostility targets openly gay public figures and a Pride event, and the actions on record are a refusal to sit at a banquet, a call for a ban, and assaults on gay men in 2005 and 2006. Nothing in the inventory documents violence against a trans person, a trans-specific legal penalty, or a trans-specific entry, document or screening rule.
tangentialFactors:
The Faroe Islands became the last Northern European country to prohibit discrimination and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, doing so only on 1 January 2007, and same-sex marriage followed a decade later in 2017 — both dates trail the rest of the Nordics.

Expression has been a recurring flashpoint. The first gay pride march in 2005 provoked much controversy. In June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter to the editor, 'Hvar eru vit á veg?', attacking the national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture', asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'. Jenis av Rana repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters and suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the centre.

Public petitioning runs in both directions. An internet petition after the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen collected 20,000 signatures in a population of about 47,000, and eight women in Tórshavn gathered a further 2,000 by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations. A petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures. In 2006 LGBT activists had gathered around 20,000 online signatures demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics; the territory had neither at that date.

Organised pushback against the hostility is also documented: Eivor Pálsdóttir's public call to ignore the 2015 demand to ban Pride, and the scale of the 2006 petition response to the Rasmussen assault.

Local political figures carry the opposition on the record: Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused the 2010 state banquet, demanded the Pride route be moved or banned in 2015, and compared LGBT Føroyar to the Sea Shepherd protesters; his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality. Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni's June 2015 letter attacked the public broadcaster's coverage and a drag show at the Nordic House.

Residents who challenged the regime faced institutional refusal: police declined to handle the 2006 Rasmus Rasmussen assault because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities, and Rasmussen died by suicide in 2012 after severe depression exacerbated by the beating. Resident petitioning on both sides is on record, including the 2,000 signatures gathered in Tórshavn shops, tourist centres and gas stations and the 1,262 signatures against same-sex marriage.

The age of consent history is local: 18 for male same-sex relations from 1933, with gender neutrality at 15 arriving only in 1988, eleven years after Denmark's 1977 change.
